cg-001.reasoning: While the Advocate makes a colorable argument under the Rogers v. Grimaldi test, the Counsel's brief more accurately reflects the practical risks facing the production. The key determining factor is that the use is 'plot-integral.' This distinguishes it from incidental background uses and heightens the risk under both prongs of a trademark claim. First, the prominence (6.9 seconds, 4% screen coverage, and plot centrality) significantly increases the danger that a court could find the use 'explicitly misleading' as to sponsorship, regardless of the production's intent. Second, and more critically, if the depiction is negative, the plot-integral nature creates a substantial risk of a trademark dilution by tarnishment claim. The reliance on Caterpillar v. Disney is misplaced; that case involved a fantastical comedy, whereas a negative portrayal in a realistic context is far more likely to be seen as damaging to the brand's goodwill. From a practical standpoint, the cost of defending a lawsuit from a large, well-funded corporation like Yum! Brands, Inc.—including the catastrophic risk of a preliminary injunction delaying the film's release—far outweighs the one-time cost of mitigation. The cost of VFX to alter the branding to a generic pizzeria is a finite and manageable expense, whereas the potential cost of litigation is open-ended and potentially ruinous. Therefore, the use is not defensible as-is; the producer must either secure a license from Pizza Hut or alter the branding.

briefs.argument: The proposed on-screen use of the 'Pizza Hut' trademark presents a material clearance risk under the Lanham Act (15 U.S.C. § 1125). While artistic works are afforded broad protection, our use is not incidental or fleeting. With 6.9 seconds of screen time, 4% screen coverage, and most critically, a 'plot-integral' function, the use moves beyond mere background 'set dressing' and becomes a focal point. This prominence creates a tangible risk that a court could find the use 'explicitly misleading' under the Rogers v. Grimaldi test, creating a false impression of affiliation, sponsorship, or endorsement by Pizza Hut and its parent, Yum! Brands, Inc. Furthermore, the plot-integral nature of the use exposes the production to a claim of trademark dilution by tarnishment if the brand is depicted in a negative, unsavory, or unwholesome context (e.g., as a site of criminal activity or a source of food poisoning). Given that the use is central to the plot, an audience is more likely to impute the fictional portrayal onto the real-world brand, damaging its goodwill. To mitigate the risk of costly litigation, a preliminary injunction delaying release, and potential damages, we must either secure a license from Yum! Brands, alter the branding to be generic, or remove the element entirely.

precedents.case_name: Rogers v. Grimaldi
precedents.holding: The use of a trademark in the title of an artistic work is permissible under the Lanham Act unless the title has (1) no artistic relevance to the underlying work, or (2) explicitly misleads as to the source or content of the work.
precedents.relevance: This is the controlling legal framework. While our use is artistically relevant (as it is 'plot_integral'), its prominence and centrality to the story create a significant risk of failing the second prong. A court could find that featuring the 'Pizza Hut' brand so directly and for a significant duration explicitly misleads the audience into believing the company sponsored or endorsed the production.

precedents.case_name: Louis Vuitton Malletier S.A. v. Warner Bros. Entm't Inc.
precedents.holding: The use of a knock-off Louis Vuitton bag in the film 'The Hangover Part II' was not infringing because the use, though for a comedic purpose, was not explicitly misleading about Louis Vuitton's affiliation with or sponsorship of the film.
precedents.relevance: This case illustrates the fact-specific nature of the 'explicitly misleading' prong of the Rogers test. Unlike the use in 'The Hangover,' which was brief and part of a character's dialogue about the item being a knock-off, our use is of the actual brand in a plot-integral way. This distinction weakens our defense and increases the risk that a court would find our use implies an affiliation that does not exist.

precedents.case_name: Caterpillar Inc. v. Walt Disney Co.
precedents.holding: The court denied Caterpillar's motion for a preliminary injunction for trademark dilution by tarnishment after its bulldozers were used by villains in the film 'George of the Jungle 2,' finding the context was fantastical and comedic and thus unlikely to harm the brand's reputation.
precedents.relevance: This case defines the risk of a tarnishment claim. If our production is a realistic drama rather than a fantasy or broad comedy, and the plot-integral use portrays Pizza Hut in a negative light (e.g., as a location for a drug deal), the risk of a successful tarnishment claim is substantially higher than it was for Disney. The 'plot-integral' nature makes the negative association more direct and damaging to the brand's reputation.

briefs.argument: Our primary defense for the use of the 'Pizza Hut' trademark is that it is a permissible use within an expressive work under the test established in Rogers v. Grimaldi. The film is an artistic, expressive work, and the use of the Pizza Hut brand is artistically relevant to the scene. Given that the use is 'plot integral,' it serves a clear narrative function, such as establishing the setting, character traits, or socioeconomic context, thereby adding a layer of realism (verisimilitude) that a fictional brand could not achieve. Secondly, the use is not explicitly misleading. The 6.9-second duration and 4% screen coverage are not excessive and do not create the impression that Yum! Brands, Inc. sponsored or endorsed this production. This is a referential use, akin to nominative fair use, where the mark is necessary to identify the real-world product being depicted. The use is reasonably necessary for that identification, and the production does nothing further to suggest an affiliation. While the defense is strong, its weakness lies in the fact that the use is not de minimis or merely incidental due to its plot integration; this elevates the need for the use to be artistically justified and not misleading, which we believe it is.

precedents.case_name: Rogers v. Grimaldi
precedents.holding: The Lanham Act does not bar the use of a trademark in an artistic work unless the use has (1) no artistic relevance to the underlying work whatsoever, or (2) if it has some artistic relevance, it explicitly misleads as to the source or content of the work.
precedents.relevance: This is the controlling legal test for use of trademarks in expressive works like our film. Our use of 'Pizza Hut' is artistically relevant for realism and is not explicitly misleading, directly satisfying the Rogers test.

precedents.case_name: Caterpillar Inc. v. Walt Disney Co.
precedents.holding: The court denied a preliminary injunction against the film 'George of the Jungle 2,' which depicted villains using Caterpillar-branded bulldozers. The court found that using real-world products lends realism to a film and that audiences are unlikely to assume sponsorship from such appearances.
precedents.relevance: This case provides a direct parallel. It affirms that the appearance of a major brand in a film, even in a negative context, does not automatically constitute infringement or dilution, especially when it serves the film's narrative realism. It supports our position that the audience will not be confused into believing Pizza Hut sponsored the production.

precedents.case_name: New Kids on the Block v. News Am. Publ'g, Inc.
precedents.holding: Established the modern test for nominative fair use, allowing the use of a trademark to refer to the trademarked good or service itself, provided: (1) the product is not readily identifiable without the mark, (2) only so much of the mark is used as is necessary, and (3) the user does nothing to suggest sponsorship or endorsement.
precedents.relevance: Our use of 'Pizza Hut' is a classic nominative use. We are referring to the actual product, which cannot be identified without its name. The prominence is limited to what is necessary for the plot, and no sponsorship is implied. This doctrine reinforces the 'referential' nature of our use under the Rogers framework.

cg-002.reasoning: While the Advocate presents a compelling and well-reasoned fair use argument, particularly regarding the transformative use of the artwork as a plot device (distinguishing it from the decorative use in 'Ringgold v. BET') and the lack of market harm due to its 'orphan work' status (supported by the logic in 'Kienitz'), the practical risks for the producer are too great. The core issue is the artwork's high prominence: at 6.9 seconds, covering 35% of the screen, and being integral to the plot, it is impossible to classify as incidental. This high 'observability' makes it a prime target for a future claim should the rights holder ever emerge. From a practical standpoint, the primary risk is not losing a potential lawsuit, but having distributors or E&O (Errors & Omissions) insurance carriers refuse to accept the film due to an uncleared, central element. The cost of litigation, even if won, can be substantial. The cost of digitally altering or replacing the artwork, while not insignificant, is a fixed, upfront expense that eliminates this unquantifiable future risk to distribution and exhibition. Therefore, to ensure the film's commercial viability, clearing the issue by removing or replacing the artwork is the only prudent course of action.

briefs.argument: The on-screen use of the 'Pizza Delivery Man' artwork presents a significant legal risk of copyright infringement and must be addressed. Under the Copyright Act of 1976 (17 U.S.C. § 101 et seq.), the creator of an original work of art holds exclusive rights, including the right to reproduce and display the work. The fact that the rights holder could not be identified does not extinguish the copyright; it merely creates an 'orphan work' situation, which does not grant a right to use. Any potential defense, such as 'de minimis' use or 'fair use', is unlikely to prevail given the nature of the work's appearance. The use is not 'de minimis' (legally insignificant) because the artwork is displayed for 6.9 seconds, covers 35% of the screen, and is integral to the plot. This level of prominence far exceeds the fleeting, out-of-focus background uses that courts have deemed de minimis. Furthermore, a 'fair use' defense under 17 U.S.C. § 107 would likely fail. The use is for a commercial purpose, it uses a creative work, the amount used is substantial and central to the scene, and it harms the potential licensing market for the artwork. The prominence and plot-integral nature of the use weigh heavily against fair use. Failure to address this issue could expose the production to litigation, injunctions, and statutory damages up to $150,000 for willful infringement (17 U.S.C. § 504). Therefore, the artwork must be licensed, digitally altered, or removed entirely.

precedents.case_name: Ringgold v. Black Entertainment Television, Inc.
precedents.holding: The court held that the unauthorized use of a copyrighted poster as set dressing in a television show, visible for a cumulative 26.75 seconds, was not de minimis use. The court emphasized that the observability, clarity, and prominence of the work were more important than mere duration.
precedents.relevance: This case establishes that even background art, if clearly visible and featured for a notable duration, is not de minimis. The 'Pizza Delivery Man' artwork, with its 35% screen coverage and plot integration, is far more prominent than the poster in 'Ringgold,' making a de minimis defense highly unlikely to succeed.

precedents.case_name: Sandoval v. New Line Cinema Corp.
precedents.holding: The court affirmed that the use of copyrighted photographs in the film 'Seven' was de minimis because they were fleeting, out of focus, and not observable to the ordinary viewer. The infringement was deemed a 'mere technical violation.'
precedents.relevance: This case provides the legal counterpoint for what constitutes de minimis use. Unlike the works in 'Sandoval', the 'Pizza Delivery Man' is clearly observable, in focus, and covers a substantial portion of the screen, rendering the use legally significant and actionable.

precedents.case_name: Gayle v. HBO
precedents.holding: The court found the use of graffiti art in the TV show 'Vinyl' to be de minimis because it was shown fleetingly, from a distance, and was indistinct. The key factor was the work's lack of 'observability' to an average viewer.
precedents.relevance: This modern case reinforces the 'observability' test for de minimis use. The prominence of the 'Pizza Delivery Man' (35% screen coverage, 6.9s duration, plot integral) ensures it is highly 'observable,' making this precedent a tool to defeat a de minimis claim, not support one.

briefs.argument:
The primary and strongest defense for the use of the 'Pizza Delivery Man' artwork is fair use under 17 U.S.C. § 107. A de minimis defense is inapplicable and likely to fail. The use, at 6.9 seconds with 35% screen coverage and being integral to the plot, is neither trivial nor incidental in the manner contemplated by cases like Ringgold v. Black Entertainment Television. The use is substantial enough to require a fair use analysis.

Our fair use argument is strong, focusing on the transformative nature of the use and the lack of market harm:

1.  **Purpose and Character of the Use:** The use is highly transformative. The artwork is not used for its original intrinsic aesthetic purpose as mere 'set dressing.' Instead, it is repurposed as a key narrative device, integral to the film's plot. This recontextualization from a static piece of art to a dynamic storytelling element creates a new work with a new purpose and message. Furthermore, a diligent, good-faith search to identify and license from the rights holder was unsuccessful. This 'orphan work' status demonstrates that the production did not intend to bypass an available market, a fact that weighs positively on the character of the use.

2.  **Nature of the Copyrighted Work:** This factor weighs against fair use, and we must be candid about this weakness. The work is a creative artistic expression, which lies at the core of copyright protection.

3.  **Amount and Substantiality Used:** The entire work is depicted. While this typically weighs against fair use, it is excusable and necessary here. To serve its transformative purpose as a plot element, the audience must be able to see and comprehend the artwork in question. Using less than the whole work would have rendered its narrative function unintelligible, aligning with precedent that allows for full reproduction when necessary for a transformative purpose (see Bill Graham Archives).

4.  **Effect on the Potential Market:** This factor strongly favors fair use. The film's brief inclusion of the art does not serve as a market substitute for the original artwork or prints of it. More importantly, regarding the licensing market, the 'orphan work' status is critical. Since the rights holder could not be located, there was no functioning, available market for the production to participate in or harm. The use does not usurp a market that the copyright holder was exploiting or could readily exploit.

precedents.case_name: Bill Graham Archives v. Dorling Kindersley Ltd.
precedents.holding: The reproduction of concert posters in a biography of the Grateful Dead was a transformative fair use. The court found that using the images as historical artifacts in a timeline was a fundamentally different purpose from the original promotional and aesthetic purpose of the posters.
precedents.relevance: This case strongly supports the argument that recontextualizing a visual work for a new purpose (e.g., historical artifact or, in our case, a plot device) is highly transformative, even if the entire work is copied. It justifies our use of the complete artwork to fulfill its new narrative function.

precedents.case_name: Ringgold v. Black Entertainment Television, Inc.
precedents.holding: The use of a copyrighted poster as set decoration in a television show, visible for a total of 27 seconds, was neither de minimis nor fair use. The court found the use was purely decorative and not transformative, serving the same aesthetic purpose as the original poster.
precedents.relevance: This case is useful to distinguish our use from an infringing one. Unlike the purely decorative, non-transformative use in Ringgold, our use of the 'Pizza Delivery Man' is integral to the plot, giving it a new, transformative purpose beyond mere decoration, thereby strengthening our fair use claim.

precedents.case_name: Kienitz v. Sconnie Nation LLC
precedents.holding: The use of a photograph of a mayor on a satirical t-shirt was deemed fair use, with the court placing significant emphasis on the fourth factor: the lack of market harm. The court reasoned the t-shirt did not act as a market substitute for the original photograph.
precedents.relevance: This precedent reinforces the importance of the market harm factor. It supports our position that because the film's use of the artwork does not substitute for the primary market for the art itself (e.g., prints or the original piece), and a licensing market could not be accessed, the fourth factor weighs heavily in favor of fair use.

cg-005.reasoning: The Advocate's fair use defense, while colorable, is unlikely to prevail in court and presents an unacceptable business risk. The core of the Advocate's argument rests on the use being 'transformative.' However, the Supreme Court's recent decision in 'Warhol v. Goldsmith' significantly narrows the scope of transformative use for commercial works that supplant a licensing market. Our use is commercial and, by incorporating a famous character for his inherent appeal, it directly competes with the rights holder's ability to license that character. This weighs the first and fourth fair use factors heavily against us. While the amount used (16.6 seconds) is quantitatively small, its plot-integral nature makes it qualitatively substantial, weakening the third-factor defense. The Counsel's position is more persuasive and pragmatic. The risk of an injunction, which could halt distribution of the entire production, is a catastrophic financial threat. This, combined with potential statutory damages up to $150,000, makes proceeding without a license untenable. The cost of defending a lawsuit, even if successful, would likely exceed the cost of a license. The argument that this is an 'orphan work' is a red flag, not a defense; the rights holder is almost certainly a major, litigious entity (Sunrise/Bandai Namco) who could surface at the most inopportune time. Therefore, the only prudent path is to either secure a license or remove/alter the character to be non-infringing.

briefs.argument: The use of the character 'Lelouch Lamperouge' in 'Untitled Production' presents a significant legal risk and constitutes likely copyright infringement. As a well-delineated, visually depicted character from the copyrighted anime series 'Code Geass,' the character itself is subject to copyright protection under 17 U.S.C. § 102. The proposed use is substantial—16.6 seconds of screen time, 30% screen coverage, and integral to the plot—and therefore cannot be dismissed as de minimis. The fact that the rights holder could not be identified does not grant a right to use the material; it classifies the character as an 'orphan work,' meaning the unknown owner could surface at any time and sue for infringement. A potential fair use defense under 17 U.S.C. § 107 would almost certainly fail. The use is for a commercial purpose, utilizes a highly creative work, is substantial in nature, and, most critically, usurps a primary licensing market for the copyright holder. An infringement claim could lead to an injunction halting distribution of our production and expose the studio to significant financial liability, including statutory damages up to $150,000 per infringed work. To mitigate this risk, the element must be licensed from the proper rights holder (likely Sunrise Inc. or Bandai Namco Filmworks), completely removed, or altered to be non-infringing.

precedents.case_name: DC Comics v. Towle
precedents.holding: The court held that a character is protectable under copyright law if it is sufficiently delineated to be recognizable as the same character whenever it appears and displays consistent, identifiable character traits and attributes. The Batmobile was found to meet this test and qualify for copyright protection.
precedents.relevance: This case affirms that a visually distinct and consistent character like 'Lelouch Lamperouge' is a copyright-protected work. Our use of the character's likeness is therefore a use of a protected work, not merely an unprotectable idea, establishing a prima facie case of copyright infringement.

precedents.case_name: Ringgold v. Black Entertainment Television, Inc.
precedents.holding: The court found that the use of a copyrighted poster as set dressing, visible for a cumulative 26.75 seconds across nine separate shots, was not a de minimis use and was therefore actionable as copyright infringement, pending a fair use analysis.
precedents.relevance: Our planned use of 'Lelouch Lamperouge' for 16.6 seconds with 30% screen coverage and plot integration is qualitatively and quantitatively significant. The Ringgold precedent makes it highly unlikely a court would consider our use to be de minimis, or too trivial to be infringing, forcing a difficult-to-win fair use defense.

precedents.case_name: Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, Inc. v. Goldsmith
precedents.holding: The Supreme Court held that the first fair use factor, 'the purpose and character of the use,' weighs against fair use when a secondary work shares a substantially similar purpose as the original and is commercial in nature, particularly when it supplants a licensing market for the original creator.
precedents.relevance: This recent Supreme Court decision severely weakens any potential fair use argument for our production. Our commercial use of 'Lelouch Lamperouge' serves the same essential purpose as the original (entertainment and character depiction) and directly harms the copyright owner's ability to license the character. This precedent makes a successful fair use defense untenable.

briefs.argument:
The use of the character 'Lelouch Lamperouge' in 'Untitled Production' constitutes a valid fair use under 17 U.S.C. § 107. While defenses like de minimis or incidental use are inapplicable due to the use being integral to the plot, a four-factor fair use analysis strongly supports our position. 

1. **Purpose and Character of the Use:** The use is transformative. 'Untitled Production' does not merely re-present the character for his original entertainment value, but rather uses him as a cultural symbol to comment on themes of rebellion, morality, and fandom. The character's inclusion is essential to our new work's message, transforming his original purpose into commentary. While the production is commercial, this is outweighed by the high degree of transformativeness. 

2. **Nature of the Copyrighted Work:** We concede this factor weighs against fair use, as the source material, 'Code Geass,' is a highly creative and fictional work at the core of copyright protection. 

3. **Amount and Substantiality Used:** The portion used—16.6 seconds of screentime—is quantitatively minimal in comparison to the hundreds of minutes comprising the original series. Qualitatively, while a main character is used, the duration is narrowly tailored and no more than necessary to achieve the specific transformative and plot-integral purpose within our production. 

4. **Effect on the Potential Market:** This factor weighs heavily in our favor. Our use does not serve as a market substitute for 'Code Geass.' It is highly improbable that an audience would watch 'Untitled Production' *instead* of the original anime. In fact, the inclusion may increase interest in the source material. Furthermore, our good-faith, albeit unsuccessful, effort to identify and contact the rights holder to negotiate a license (an 'orphan work' situation) demonstrates that we are not attempting to usurp an established licensing market for this type of use. 

In conclusion, the transformative purpose of the use and the lack of any discernible market harm strongly favor a finding of fair use, despite the creative nature of the source work.

precedents.case_name: Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, Inc.
precedents.holding: A commercial parody can qualify as fair use, as it can be transformative by adding new expression, meaning, or message. The more transformative the new work, the less will be the significance of other factors, like commercialism, that may weigh against a finding of fair use.
precedents.relevance: This seminal Supreme Court case establishes that a commercial use can be transformative and thus fair use. It provides the core of our argument that our use of Lelouch Lamperouge is a transformative commentary, not a market substitute, which is the central question of the fair use inquiry.

precedents.case_name: Bill Graham Archives v. Dorling Kindersley Ltd.
precedents.holding: The use of seven reduced-size images of concert posters in a biographical book was a transformative fair use. The use was for a new historical and illustrative purpose, and though the entire images were copied, they were used in a limited and necessary way.
precedents.relevance: This case supports our argument on the third factor ('Amount and Substantiality'). It shows that even using an entire work (in that case, posters) can be fair use if the use is for a new, transformative purpose and is scaled appropriately for that purpose. Our 16.6-second use is similarly tailored to our new narrative and commentary purpose.

precedents.case_name: Ringgold v. Black Entertainment Television, Inc.
precedents.holding: The use of a copyrighted poster as set dressing in a television show, visible for a total of 27 seconds, was not de minimis and required a full fair use analysis (which the court suggested would fail).
precedents.relevance: This precedent candidly shows the weakness of a 'de minimis' defense for a use of this duration and prominence. It underscores why we must rely on the more robust, fact-intensive fair use defense. Our use, being plot-integral, is even more significant than the background set dressing in Ringgold, making a fair use argument essential.

The 11.7-second screen time falls into a risky grey area between the non-infringing use in Sandoval and the infringing use in Ringgold. However, the dispositive issue here is a practical and financial one. The inability to identify the rights holder makes it impossible to obtain a license, which is a prerequisite for securing Errors & Omissions (E&O) insurance coverage for this element. Proceeding without clearance means the production would bear 100% of the liability for any future infringement claim. The potential cost of defending a lawsuit and, more critically, the catastrophic business risk of a court-ordered injunction to halt distribution, far outweighs the one-time, manageable cost of digitally altering or removing the painting in post-production. The prudent and standard industry practice is to eliminate this uninsurable risk by clearing the item.

briefs.argument: The on-screen use of the 'Framed Painting' constitutes a significant legal risk that must be addressed by removing or altering the artwork. While the use is not plot-integral, its 11.7 seconds of screen time is substantial enough to fail a *de minimis* use defense, which requires the use to be so trivial as to be legally insignificant. The core of the risk stems from The Copyright Act (17 U.S.C. § 106), which grants copyright owners the exclusive right to reproduce and display their work. Our unauthorized inclusion of the painting is a prima facie infringement of these rights. A court would likely reject a *de minimis* defense based on the precedent set in *Ringgold v. Black Entertainment Television, Inc.*, where a background poster visible for a comparable amount of time was found to be infringing. The artwork in our production is sufficiently observable to be recognizable, unlike in cases like *Sandoval v. New Line Cinema*, where the works were obscured and out of focus. Furthermore, a fair use defense is unlikely to succeed given the commercial nature of our production and the creative nature of the artwork. The most critical factor is that the rights holder could not be identified. This prevents us from obtaining a license and, crucially, means we cannot secure Errors & Omissions (E&O) insurance for this element. The emergence of an unknown rights holder post-release could lead to a demand for a preliminary injunction to halt distribution—a catastrophic outcome far more costly than addressing the issue in production. Therefore, to mitigate legal and financial risk, the painting must be removed or digitally altered to be non-infringing.

The 11.7 seconds of screen time for the 'Framed Painting' is substantial enough to fall under the *Ringgold* standard, making a *de minimis* defense extremely risky.

precedents.case_name: The Copyright Act of 1976

precedents.relevance: Our inclusion of the 'Framed Painting' in the final cut of the production is a reproduction and a public display. precedents.holding: The court ruled that the use of copyrighted photographs in the background of the film 'Seven' was *de minimis* because the works were shown for brief durations, were out of focus, and were not clearly discernible to the ordinary observer.
precedents.relevance: This case defines the threshold for a successful *de minimis* defense. For the defense to apply, the work must be essentially unrecognizable. The 'Framed Painting' in our production, at 2% screen coverage, is likely clear enough to be identified, distinguishing it from the facts in *Sandoval* and making a claim of infringement more likely to succeed.

briefs.argument: The strongest good-faith defense for the use of the 'Framed Painting' is that the use is de minimis—so trivial as to not constitute copyright infringement. The painting appears for only 11.7 seconds, occupies a mere 2% of the screen, is not a focal point of the action, and is entirely irrelevant to the plot, serving only as background set dressing. This type of incidental, background use to establish a realistic setting has been found to be non-infringing. The primary precedent supporting this is Gottlieb Development LLC v. Paramount, where the background use of a pinball machine was deemed de minimis. Similarly, in Sandoval v. New Line Cinema, the use of photographs that were indistinct and out of focus in the background was found de minimis. The primary weakness in this defense is the 11.7-second duration, which is longer than in some classic de minimis cases. A court might look to Ringgold v. Black Entertainment Television, which found 27 seconds of screen time for a poster was not de minimis. However, our use is distinguishable from Ringgold because the painting here is generic background, unlike the thematically important poster in that case, and the screen time is less than half. While the inability to identify the rights holder is not a legal defense, it demonstrates our good faith in being unable to seek a license. Should a de minimis argument fail, a fair use defense would be a weaker alternative.

precedents.holding: The court held that the background, partially-obscured use of a copyrighted pinball machine in a movie scene for brief moments was de minimis and therefore not copyright infringement, as it was merely part of the set dressing.

precedents.case_name: Ringgold v. Black Entertainment Television, Inc.
precedents.holding: The court found that the use of a copyrighted poster in a TV show's set for a total of 27 seconds, sometimes in full view, was not de minimis, considering the work's prominence and thematic relevance to the set decoration.
precedents.relevance: This case represents the primary risk to our de minimis defense, as it sets a low threshold for what constitutes more than trivial use. cg-007.reasoning: The court finds the arguments for requiring clearance to be overwhelmingly persuasive. Both parties correctly identify Ringgold v. Black Entertainment Television, Inc. as a key precedent, and its application strongly disfavors the production. A 6-second use at 20% screen coverage is not de minimis; it is prominent and recognizable. The advocate's primary defense hinges on a 'transformative' fair use argument, likening the use to set dressing that provides cultural context, per Bill Graham Archives. Unlike the historical posters in Bill Graham, using a well-known, contemporary anime character's image is not a commentary or historical record; it is a decorative use that exploits the character's existing appeal. This directly implicates the fourth fair use factor: market harm. A robust licensing market exists for exactly this type of use (e.g., posters on a character's wall). From a practical standpoint, the cost of litigating a 'defensible' but high-risk fair use claim against a notoriously litigious rights holder like Bandai Namco—with the potential for a production-halting injunction and statutory damages up to $150,000—dwarfs the likely cost of either securing a license or paying for a VFX fix to replace the image. The risk is not commercially reasonable. Therefore, the element must be licensed or removed.

Failure to clear this use exposes the production to the risk of an injunction, significant statutory damages (up to $150,000 per willful infringement), and attorney's fees. e6f7d08b-c9a1-4e4b-a2e1-5f2b8b9c9d9a.note: No statutory incidental-inclusion exception; de minimis is judge-made and fact-specific.

e6f7d08b-c9a1-4e4b-a2e1-5f2b8b9c9d9a.name: Moral rights (a risk, not a defence)
e6f7d08b-c9a1-4e4b-a2e1-5f2b8b9c9d9a.authority: CPI art. L.121-1 — droit moral is perpetual, inalienable and imprescriptible; it survives sale of the copyright
e6f7d08b-c9a1-4e4b-a2e1-5f2b8b9c9d9a.note: Perpetual and inalienable here: the author can object to treatment of the work even after selling the copyright, and heirs can assert it without time limit.

e6f7d08b-c9a1-4e4b-a2e1-5f2b8b9c9d9a.name: Parody / caricature
e6f7d08b-c9a1-4e4b-a2e1-5f2b8b9c9d9a.authority: No statutory parody exception. The Parody Montage case (Supreme Court, 1980) treated unauthorised parody as infringement of the integrity right
e6f7d08b-c9a1-4e4b-a2e1-5f2b8b9c9d9a.note: No statutory parody exception here. Any parody argument runs through criticism, review or free expression instead — an argument to be made, not a safe harbour to rely on.

e6f7d08b-c9a1-4e4b-a2e1-5f2b8b9c9d9a.name: Fair use (open-ended)
e6f7d08b-c9a1-4e4b-a2e1-5f2b8b9c9d9a.authority: Copyright Act arts. 30-50 — enumerated limitations only
e6f7d08b-c9a1-4e4b-a2e1-5f2b8b9c9d9a.note: Closed list: a use that is not on the statutory list is infringing however reasonable it looks. A fair-use memo written for the US does not travel here.
